File
Size

447 MB
made for this course (see below); from the teacher
89f132ff5af712356e4cefdcc1a6cf68

103 MB
https://farm.cse.ucdavis.edu/~ctbrown/sourmash-db.new/gtdb-rs226/gtdb-rs226.lineages.csv
519293f254dfa763c6f30473d1e3e952



What the file is. gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip contains one sourmash sketch (k = 31) for each of the 143,384 species-representative genomes of GTDB release 226. It is a reduced copy of the official sourmash database gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.dna.zip (3.9 GB), listed on the sourmash databases page.
Why it is reduced. The official file keeps 1 k-mer in 1,000 of each genome (scaled=1000). Searching it takes 6 minutes per bin, or 6 GB of memory with the fast search. The course file keeps 1 k-mer in 10,000 (scaled=10000): the search takes 1 minute per bin and less than 1 GB of memory. On the course data it gives the same species for every bin as the official file.
How to use it. Sketch your genomes with the same settings, -p k=31,scaled=10000, then run sourmash gather and sourmash tax genome as in the assembly and binning tutorial.
How it was made. Anyone can rebuild it from the official file (8 minutes, 4.5 GB of memory):
curl -f -O https://farm.cse.ucdavis.edu/~ctbrown/sourmash-db.new/gtdb-rs226/gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.dna.zip
sourmash sig downsample --scaled 10000 gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.dna.zip -o gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip
Limits. A sketch this small is made for whole genomes and bins of 1 Mb or more. Do not use it for short contigs or for reads.
Licence. The two files can be copied and shared, with credit.

The taxonomy comes from GTDB, which is under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 licence (CC BY-SA 4.0): you may copy and adapt it if you give credit, link to the licence, say what you changed, and share your version under the same licence.
The sketches were computed by the sourmash team and are marked CC0 (no restriction) inside the file.
So the course file is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. Credit: “GTDB release 226 (Parks et al., https://gtdb.ecogenomic.org); sketches from the sourmash project (https://sourmash.readthedocs.io); reduced to scaled = 10000 for the course Introduction to Metagenomics”.

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
ImportantBefore you start



Do the Setup first. Then open a terminal and activate the tools of the course:
cd ~/mag2026/Metagenomics_course
pixi shell
In this tutorial you’ll learn how to inspect assemble metagenomic data and retrieve draft genomes from assembled metagenomes
We’ll use a mock community of 10 bacteria sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq. In reality the data were simulated using InSilicoSeq.
The 10 bacteria in the dataset were selected from the Tara Ocean study that recovered 957 distinct Metagenome-assembled-genomes (or MAGs) that were previsouly unknown! (full list on figshare )

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
section: Prepare and organise your working directory
text:
Prepare and organise your working directory
All the work of this tutorial is done in the folder ~/mag2026/d2, organised like the one of Day 1: the reads go in data/, everything you compute goes in results/. Every command below is run from ~/mag2026/d2, unless the text says otherwise.
mkdir -p ~/mag2026/d2
cd ~/mag2026/d2
mkdir data
mkdir results
If you close your terminal and come back later, activate the tools again (see the top of this page) and return to the folder with cd ~/mag2026/d2.

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Getting the Data
cd ~/mag2026/d2/data
curl -f -O -J -L https://osf.io/th9z6/download
curl -f -O -J -L https://osf.io/k6vme/download
chmod -w tara_reads_R*
cd ~/mag2026/d2
The two files of reads are now in data/. The chmod -w command protects them: they can be read, but not changed or deleted by mistake.






NoteIf the download fails



The option -f makes curl stop with an error message (for example curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 500) when the server has a problem. Without it, curl would save the error page of the server under the name of the file, and the next command would fail in a confusing way. If you see such an error, wait a few minutes and run the command again, or copy the file from the drive of your teacher. The Data page gives the checksum of every file.

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Quality Control
we’ll use FastQC to check the quality of our data, as well as sickle for trimming the bad quality part of the reads.
mkdir -p results/fastqc
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc data/tara_reads_*.fastq.gz
Open the two reports of results/fastqc in your web browser.






TipQuestion



What is the average read length? The average quality?








TipQuestion



Compared to single genome sequencing, what graphs differ?


Now we’ll trim the reads using sickle
sickle pe -f data/tara_reads_R1.fastq.gz -r data/tara_reads_R2.fastq.gz -t sanger \
    -o results/tara_trimmed_R1.fastq -p results/tara_trimmed_R2.fastq -s /dev/null






TipQuestion



How many reads were trimmed?

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Assembly
Megahit will be used for the assembly.
megahit -1 results/tara_trimmed_R1.fastq -2 results/tara_trimmed_R2.fastq -o results/tara_assembly
the resulting assembly can be found under results/tara_assembly/final.contigs.fa.






TipQuestion



How many contigs does this assembly contain?

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Binning
First we need to map the reads back against the assembly to get coverage information. We map the trimmed reads, the same reads that were used for the assembly. The mapping takes about 4 minutes.
bowtie2-build results/tara_assembly/final.contigs.fa results/final.contigs
bowtie2 -p 2 -x results/final.contigs \
    -1 results/tara_trimmed_R1.fastq -2 results/tara_trimmed_R2.fastq | \
    samtools view -bS -o results/tara_to_sort.bam
samtools sort results/tara_to_sort.bam -o results/tara.bam
samtools index results/tara.bam
then we run metabat
runMetaBat.sh -m 1500 --seed 1 results/tara_assembly/final.contigs.fa results/tara.bam
mv final.contigs.fa.metabat-bins* results/metabat
mv final.contigs.fa.depth.txt results/






NoteWhy --seed 1?



MetaBAT 2 makes some of its choices at random. Without a seed, two runs on exactly the same files give slightly different bins: a few contigs change bin. The option --seed fixes the starting point of the random choices (any number works; we all use 1), so the same input gives the same bins every time.
In this course we fix the seed so that everybody gets bins with the same content, and we can discuss them together.
One thing still differs between laptops: the numbers of the bins. The assembler gives its contigs other names, in another order, at each run, so your bin.3 can be the bin.7 of your neighbour, with exactly the same contigs inside. To recognise a bin, look at its size and its number of contigs, not at its number:
seqkit stats results/metabat/bin.*.fa
In a research project the answer has two parts.

Do fix the seed and write it in your methods, with the version of the tool: without it, nobody can reproduce your bins exactly, not even you.
Do not believe that a fixed seed makes the bins more correct. It only hides the variation. To see it, run the binning a few times with different seeds: the bins that stay the same are robust, and the contigs that move from one bin to another are uncertain.

And never try several seeds to keep the one that gives the result you prefer.


MetaBAT 2 writes its output in the current folder: a table with the coverage of each contig (final.contigs.fa.depth.txt) and a folder of bins, whose name ends with the date and time of the run. The two mv commands put them in results/, and rename the folder of bins to metabat. Each bin is one FASTA file, bin.1.fa, bin.2.fa, and so on.






TipQuestion



How many bins did we obtain?

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
section: Checking the quality of the bins
text:
Checking the quality of the bins
A bin is only a draft genome. Before using it, we estimate two numbers:

completeness: which part of the genome is in the bin;
contamination: how much of the bin comes from other genomes.

Nobody knows the true genome, so both numbers are estimates. They are based on genes that almost every bacterium has in exactly one copy (single-copy marker genes): a missing marker lowers the completeness, a marker found twice raises the contamination.
We will use two tools that make this estimate in different ways, and compare them:

CheckM (version 1) places each bin in a reference tree and counts the marker genes of its lineage;
CheckM2 predicts the two numbers with machine-learning models trained on many genomes.

Each tool has its own environment and its own reference data.

CheckM
Open a second terminal and activate the CheckM environment:
cd ~/mag2026/Metagenomics_course
pixi shell -e checkm1
cd ~/mag2026/d2
The first time you run checkm you have to get its reference data (289 MB; ask your teacher for the drive copy) and tell CheckM where they are:
mkdir -p ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
cd ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
curl -f -O https://data.ace.uq.edu.au/public/CheckM_databases/checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
# check the download: the result must be 631012fa598c43fdeb88c619ad282c4d
md5sum checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
tar -xzf checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
rm checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
checkm data setRoot ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
cd ~/mag2026/d2
Now run CheckM on the folder of bins (about 5 minutes):
checkm lineage_wf -t 2 --gplace_max_memory 2G -x fa results/metabat results/checkm
checkm qa results/checkm/lineage.ms results/checkm --tab_table -f results/checkm.tsv






Note



--gplace_max_memory 2G limits the memory of the step that places the bins in the reference tree. Without this limit, CheckM needs far more memory than a laptop has and is stopped by the system (“Killed”).


The result is the table results/checkm.tsv. Columns 12 and 13 are the completeness and the contamination:
cut -f1,12,13 results/checkm.tsv
The other columns give the lineage that CheckM chose for the bin, and how many marker genes were found 0, 1, 2 or more times.


CheckM2
In the same second terminal, leave the CheckM environment and activate the CheckM2 environment:
exit
pixi shell -e checkm2
cd ~/mag2026/d2
The first time, get the CheckM2 database (1.7 GB to download, 2.9 GB on disk; ask your teacher for the drive copy):
cd ~/mag2026/databases
curl -f -L -o checkm2_database.tar.gz "https://zenodo.org/records/14897628/files/checkm2_database.tar.gz?download=1"
# check the download: the result must be 07c10655620843b517d0df0c160d911f
md5sum checkm2_database.tar.gz
tar -xzf checkm2_database.tar.gz
rm checkm2_database.tar.gz
cd ~/mag2026/d2
Run CheckM2 on the same bins (about 8 minutes):
checkm2 predict --lowmem --threads 2 -x fa \
    --input results/metabat --output-directory results/checkm2 \
    --database_path ~/mag2026/databases/CheckM2_database/uniref100.KO.1.dmnd






Note



--lowmem makes CheckM2 use less memory, at the price of a longer run. Without it, CheckM2 does not fit in 6 GB.


The result is the table results/checkm2/quality_report.tsv. Its first three columns are the name of the bin, the completeness and the contamination:
cut -f1-3 results/checkm2/quality_report.tsv


Compare the two tools
Put the completeness and contamination of both tools side by side, for example in a spreadsheet or on paper.






TipQuestion



Do CheckM and CheckM2 agree? For which bins do they differ the most?








TipQuestion



The two tools were given exactly the same bins. Why can their estimates differ? Which one is “right”?


To decide which bins are good enough, many studies use the MIMAG standard (Bowers et al. 2017):









Quality
Completeness
Contamination
Also required




High-quality draft
more than 90%
less than 5%
the 23S, 16S and 5S rRNA genes and at least 18 tRNAs


Medium-quality draft
50% or more
less than 10%



Low-quality draft
less than 50%
less than 10%










TipQuestion



Which bins should we keep for downstream analysis? Give each bin its MIMAG quality, once with the CheckM values and once with the CheckM2 values. Does a bin change category?








TipQuestion



Both tools estimate contamination from marker genes that are found more than once. Imagine a bin that contains a few contigs of another organism, and these contigs carry no marker gene. What would the tools report? What does this tell you about a contamination of “2%”?








Note



Our reads were simulated from 10 known genomes, and the name of each read still says which genome it comes from. So for this dataset the truth can be checked. Ask your teacher how the bins compare with the truth, after you have answered the questions.








NoteIf CheckM or CheckM2 does not run on your laptop



Tell your teacher. There are two other ways to get the results:

Result files. The teacher gives you checkm.tsv and quality_report.tsv, computed on the same data. Use them for the comparison.
Galaxy. Upload your 10 bin files (results/metabat/bin.*.fa, 20 MB) to usegalaxy.eu, make a collection of them, and run the tools “CheckM lineage_wf” and “CheckM2” on it.



When you have finished, close the second terminal, or type exit to leave the environment.

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Functional annotation
Now we should have a collection of MAGs that we can further analyze. The first step is to predict genes as right now we only have raw genomic sequences. We will use Prokka, a widely used annotation tool for prokaryotic genomes.
This tool does gene prediction as well as some decent and useful annotations, and is actually quite easy to run!
Prokka is in its own environment. Open a second terminal (or reuse the one of CheckM, after exit) and activate it:
cd ~/mag2026/Metagenomics_course
pixi shell -e prokka
cd ~/mag2026/d2
On a Mac with Apple Silicon, this environment runs through Rosetta: see Setup.
Choose one bin, for example a bin with a high completeness and a low contamination, and annotate it (about 3 minutes; replace bin.1 and bin1 by your choice):
prokka --cpus 2 --outdir results/prokka_bin1 --prefix bin1 results/metabat/bin.1.fa
Prokka produces a number of output files in the folder results/prokka_bin1, which mostly represent the same thing in different formats:







File
Content




bin1.txt
a summary: number of contigs, genes (CDS), tRNA and rRNA genes


bin1.faa
the predicted proteins (FASTA). You need this file for eggNOG-mapper


bin1.ffn
the predicted genes (FASTA, DNA)


bin1.gff
the position and the annotation of every gene on the contigs


bin1.tsv
a table with one line per gene



Prokka also renames all the sequences with nicer IDs.
cat results/prokka_bin1/bin1.txt
grep -c "hypothetical protein" results/prokka_bin1/bin1.faa






TipQuestion



How many genes (CDS) did Prokka find? How many of them are “hypothetical proteins”? What does “hypothetical” mean here?








TipQuestion



Every bacterium has rRNA genes (16S, 23S, 5S) and a full set of tRNA genes. Look at the summary of your bin: is something missing? Why would these genes be absent from a bin, even when the bin is almost complete?



eggNOG-mapper (on Galaxy)
The annotations of Prokka are good but not very complete for environmental bacteria. eggNOG-mapper compares each protein with the eggNOG database of groups of related genes (orthologous groups), and transfers their annotation: gene names, functional categories (COG), pathways (KEGG) and more. This is a bit heavier in computation.
The eggNOG database takes more than 40 GB, too much for a laptop. So this step runs on Galaxy, not on your computer.

Choose one MAG (don’t be greedy, it is not fast!). You need its protein file: the .faa file that Prokka made for this MAG.
Log in to usegalaxy.eu and upload the .faa file with the “Upload” button.
Search the tool panel for “eggNOG Mapper” and run the tool on your file. Keep the default settings.
Wait until the job is green, then open the annotation table.

usegalaxy.eu runs eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13 with version 5.0.2 of the eggNOG database. Write these two versions down: they are part of your result.






TipQuestion



OPTIONAL: understand the output. Find three proteins that Prokka named “hypothetical protein”. What does eggNOG-mapper say about them?








NoteIf Galaxy is slow or not available



The authors of eggNOG-mapper offer a web service: https://eggnog-mapper.cgmlab.org (the old address, eggnog-mapper.embl.de, sends you there). Upload the same .faa file and follow the instructions of the page. Submit your job early: jobs wait in a queue, and a job can take an hour or more. The web service uses a newer database (eggNOG 7), so some annotations differ from the Galaxy result.

title: Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning
text:
Taxonomic annotation
We now know more about the genes your MAG contains, however we do not really know who we have?! checkm might have given us an indication but it is only approximative.
Taxonomic classification for full genomes is not always easy for MAGs, often the 16S gene is missing as it assembles badly, and which other genes to use to for taxonomy is not always evident. Typically marker genes, min-hashes or k-mer databases are used as reference. It is often problematic for environmental data as the databases are not biased into our direction! We will use a min-hash database of the GTDB representative genomes with a tool called sourmash.
GTDB is a taxonomy built from genomes. It contains one representative genome per species, including many species known only from MAGs. sourmash keeps a small “sketch” of each genome: a sample of its k-mers. Comparing two sketches is very fast.

Get the database
The database of this tutorial is a reduced copy of the sourmash database “GTDB R226, species representatives, k=31”, made for this course so that it fits in the memory of a laptop. Your teacher gives you the two files on a drive:

gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip (447 MB): the sketches of the 143,384 GTDB representative genomes;
gtdb-rs226.lineages.csv (103 MB): the taxonomy of each genome.

Copy them into ~/mag2026/databases/sourmash/. The Data page explains how the reduced file was made and how to rebuild it.
SOURMASH_DB=~/mag2026/databases/sourmash
ls $SOURMASH_DB


Sketch the bins and search the database
sourmash is in the main environment (the first terminal). For each bin we make a sketch (sourmash sketch), then search the genomes of the database that best explain it (sourmash gather). This takes about 1 minute per bin.
cd ~/mag2026/d2
mkdir -p results/sourmash
for i in results/metabat/bin.*.fa
do
    name=$(basename $i .fa)
    echo $name
    sourmash sketch dna -p k=31,scaled=10000 --name $name $i -o results/sourmash/${name}.sig
    sourmash gather results/sourmash/${name}.sig $SOURMASH_DB/gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip \
        -o results/sourmash/${name}.gather.csv
done
For each bin, gather prints the genomes it found and which part of the bin they explain. If nothing in the database is similar enough, it prints “No matches” and writes no file.


From genomes to a taxonomy
sourmash tax genome reads the matches and the taxonomy file, and gives one classification per bin:
sourmash tax genome -g results/sourmash/*.gather.csv -t $SOURMASH_DB/gtdb-rs226.lineages.csv \
    -o results/sourmash/bins --output-format csv_summary human
cat results/sourmash/bins.human.txt
The lineage is written with the GTDB prefixes: d__ domain, p__ phylum, c__ class, o__ order, f__ family, g__ genus, s__ species.






TipQuestion



How many bins received a classification? At which rank? Look at the species names: what do names such as sp002699365 tell you about these organisms?








TipQuestion



One bin has no match. Does that mean the bin is bad? Compare with its CheckM results before you answer.


The GTDB database is also used by the tool GTDB-Tk. It uses marker genes and places each genome in a reference tree. It is more sensitive, but its database is far too large for a laptop.






NoteOptional



Run GTDB-Tk on Galaxy: upload your bins to usegalaxy.eu and search the tool panel for “GTDB-Tk Classify genomes”. Compare its answer with the one of sourmash.

title: Day 1: read-based taxonomy (assembly-free)
text:
Functional Classification
So far we asked “who is there?”. Shotgun reads can also answer “what can they do?”: the reads are compared with databases of genes and pathways. A widely used tool is HUMAnN (version 3; the older HUMAnN2 is no longer maintained). Its databases are too large for this tutorial. You will meet HUMAnN on Galaxy, in the metatranscriptomics tutorial of Day 3.






NoteCredits



This tutorial is shared teaching material, co-developed with Hadrien Gourlé. It started from his tutorial Whole Metagenome Sequencing. See Licence and credits.

title: Project
text: From the afternoon of Day 3, you work on an individual project. On Day 5 you present it.

title: Project
text:
Grade breakdown

40% Active participation
20% Project report
40% Pre-Project presentation and discussion

title: Project
text:
The project

Instructions
Find a tool, pipeline, or analysis method of metagenomics that has not been seen during the course and test and evaluate it. You must explain how it works, how you found it, and its use in metagenomics studies. You can compare it to a similar tool/method seen during the course.
You are tasked to have a report of at least two pages (not counting graphics, pictures, and tables). Additional points will be provided if your work is easily reproducible (scripts, command list, and workflows provided in addition to the report).


Project grade breakdown

10% originality
20% Reasoning and Explanation of what it should do
30% execution and testing
20% analysis of the results
20% comparison to existing methods

title: Project
text:
Presentation plan
You will present your individual project and a summary of the course.
15 minutes of group presentation where you summarise the principles and methods of metagenomics.
15 minutes of individual presentation where you expose your work:

Methods selected and Why
Results
Discussion (comparison with a method seen during the course)

title: Project
text:
Use of AI tools

Tutorials: not allowed. You follow the instructions and think about the questions yourself.
Written report: not allowed. The report is written by you.
Project work: allowed as a support, not to do the work for you.
Presentation: made by you. You may use AI to generate images.

title: Setup
text: We do the setup together in class on Day 1. This page is the reference.

title: Setup
text:
What you need

A laptop with at least 8 GB of memory (RAM) and 50 GB of free disk space.
Windows 10 or 11 with WSL (Ubuntu), or Linux, or macOS.
An internet connection for the first installation (about 3 GB of downloads for the tools).

The local tutorials run in a Linux terminal: the Ubuntu terminal of WSL on Windows, or the Terminal on Linux and macOS.

title: Setup
text:
Windows: WSL
The local tutorials run in WSL 2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) with Ubuntu. If WSL is not installed yet: open PowerShell as administrator, run the command below, and restart the computer.
wsl --install

title: Setup
text:
Troubleshooting

“HTTP error” or “could not resolve host” in WSL
Sometimes WSL loses its connection to the internet, and pixi install, curl or git clone stop with an HTTP or “could not resolve host” error. The usual cause is the network or DNS setting of WSL, not the tool. Try these steps in order, and test after each one.
Test. In the Ubuntu terminal, this command must print an address:
getent hosts conda.anaconda.org
Step 1: restart WSL. In PowerShell, run wsl --shutdown, then open Ubuntu again. If that is not enough, restart the computer.
Step 2 (Windows 11): use the network of Windows. Open the WSL settings file from PowerShell with notepad "$env:USERPROFILE\.wslconfig" and add the two network lines under [wsl2]. Keep the memory line if you have one.
[wsl2]
networkingMode=mirrored
dnsTunneling=true
Save, run wsl --shutdown in PowerShell, open Ubuntu again and repeat the test. This setting needs Windows 11 version 22H2 or later. It also helps when a VPN is active.
Step 3 (last resort): set the DNS server by hand. Ask your teacher before you do this.

In Ubuntu, open the WSL configuration with sudo nano /etc/wsl.conf and add:
[network]
generateResolvConf = false
In PowerShell, run wsl --shutdown, then open Ubuntu again.
In Ubuntu, write a public DNS server in the DNS file:
sudo rm -f /etc/resolv.conf
echo "nameserver 1.1.1.1" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf



A warning about “post-link scripts” during pixi install
Pixi does not run the small scripts that some packages (here Krona) would like to run after their installation, and it tells you so. This warning is harmless: the tools of the course work without these scripts.


FastQC prints “usage: fastqc …” and stops when you use -o
Recent versions of FastQC no longer accept the short option -o for the output folder. Use the long form, as in the tutorials: fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ....


A step is “Killed” or stops without a message
The step probably needed more memory than Linux has. Check the memory with free -h and see Give WSL 6 GB of memory. Close other programs and run the step again.

A one-week course on the analysis of microbial communities by sequencing: amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics (read-based, and with assembly and binning), long reads and metatranscriptomics.
The week has lectures and practicals for two and a half days, then an individual project. Each practical exists in two forms: a local tutorial on your laptop, and a Galaxy tutorial on usegalaxy.eu. The whole class follows the same one; the teacher says which.

section: What differs between the two routes
text:
What differs between the two routes

Databases. A result depends on the reference database and on its version. The local Day 1 tutorial uses the Kraken 2 database Standard-8 of October 2026. The Galaxy tutorial uses a larger database (PlusPF), and the Standard-8 database on usegalaxy.eu dates from June 2022. Expect different numbers, and always write down the database and its version.
Tools. The Galaxy binning tutorial uses several binners and refines their bins; the local tutorial uses one binner (MetaBAT 2). The local DADA2 tutorial uses SILVA 138.2; the Galaxy DADA2 tutorial uses the SILVA release installed on Galaxy (132), which still has the old names of the phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes).
Waiting time. On Galaxy your jobs wait in a queue with the jobs of other users. Start the long jobs before a break.

The GTN tutorials are updated regularly. The links were checked on 12 November 2026.

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
This tutorial is aimed at being a walkthrough of the DADA2 pipeline. It uses the data of the now famous MiSeq SOP by the Mothur authors but analyses the data using DADA2.
DADA2 is a relatively new method to analyse amplicon data which uses exact variants instead of OTUs.
The advantages of the DADA2 method is described in the paper

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Before Starting
There are two ways to follow this tutorial in RStudio:

copy and paste the code blocks below into R, one at a time; or
download this page as a notebook (right-click, “Save link as”), open it in RStudio and run the chunks one by one.

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Install and Load Packages
This tutorial runs in RStudio, with R 4.5 or newer. Check your version with R.version.string.
First install DADA2 and the other packages. Run the lines one by one. The installation takes several minutes. If R asks “Update all/some/none?”, answer n (none).
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("dada2", "phyloseq", "DECIPHER"))
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "phangorn"))
BiocManager installs the version of DADA2 that belongs to your version of R: DADA2 1.38 with R 4.5, DADA2 1.40 with R 4.6. This tutorial was tested with DADA2 1.38.
Now load the packages and look at your DADA2 version. Write it down: it is part of your methods
library(dada2)
library(ggplot2)
library(phyloseq)
library(phangorn)
library(DECIPHER)
packageVersion('dada2')

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Download the Data
You will also need to download the data, as well as the SILVA database. The downloads are done from R, so this works the same way on Windows, macOS and Linux. The files are saved in the working directory of R. Keep the work of this tutorial in one folder, as for the other tutorials:

Create a folder for this tutorial, for example mag2026/d2_amplicon in your Documents.
If you use the notebook: save it in this folder and open it from there. R then works in this folder.
If you copy and paste the code: in RStudio, choose this folder with the menu Session, Set Working Directory, Choose Directory.

Check where R works with getwd().
# large files: allow up to 10 minutes per download
options(timeout = 600)

# the MiSeq SOP data (37 MB)
download.file('https://mothur.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/wiki/miseqsopdata.zip',
              'miseqsopdata.zip', mode = 'wb')
# check that the download is complete:
# the result must be 98144f5057628139271d94612bb27d96
tools::md5sum('miseqsopdata.zip')
unzip('miseqsopdata.zip')

# the SILVA reference files (release 138.2), placed in the data folder
# 140 MB and 70 MB: this can take a few minutes
download.file('https://zenodo.org/records/14169026/files/silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz',
              'MiSeq_SOP/silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz', mode = 'wb')
download.file('https://zenodo.org/records/14169026/files/silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz',
              'MiSeq_SOP/silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz', mode = 'wb')
# check the downloads: the results must be
# 1764e2a36b4500ccb1c7d5261948a414 and 62fd939bd1aa9832d2089847f9f0b87d
tools::md5sum(c('MiSeq_SOP/silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz',
                'MiSeq_SOP/silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz'))
Then check that you have downloaded the data
path <- 'MiSeq_SOP'
list.files(path)

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Filtering and Trimming
First we create two lists with the sorted name of the reads: one for the forward reads, one for the reverse reads
raw_forward <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R1_001.fastq",
                               full.names=TRUE))

raw_reverse <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R2_001.fastq",
                               full.names=TRUE))

# we also need the sample names
sample_names <- sapply(strsplit(basename(raw_forward), "_"),
                       `[`,  # extracts the first element of a subset
                       1)
then we visualise the quality of our reads
plotQualityProfile(raw_forward[1:2])
plotQualityProfile(raw_reverse[1:2])
The forward reads are good quality (although dropping a bit at the end as usual) while the reverse are way worse.
Based on these profiles, we will truncate the forward reads at position 240 and the reverse reads at position 160 where the quality distribution crashes.
Dada2 requires us to define the name of our output files
# place filtered files in filtered/ subdirectory
filtered_path <- file.path(path, "filtered")

filtered_forward <- file.path(filtered_path,
                              paste0(sample_names, "_R1_trimmed.fastq.gz"))

filtered_reverse <- file.path(filtered_path,
                              paste0(sample_names, "_R2_trimmed.fastq.gz"))
We’ll use standard filtering parameters: maxN=0 (DADA22 requires no Ns), truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE and maxEE=2. The maxEE parameter sets the maximum number of “expected errors” allowed in a read, which according to the USEARCH authors is a better filter than simply averaging quality scores.
out <- filterAndTrim(raw_forward, filtered_forward, raw_reverse,
                     filtered_reverse, truncLen=c(240,160), maxN=0,
                     maxEE=c(2,2), truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE, compress=TRUE,
                     multithread=TRUE)
head(out)

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Learn the Error Rates
The DADA2 algorithm depends on a parametric error model and every amplicon dataset has a slightly different error rate. The learnErrors of Dada2 learns the error model from the data and will help DADA2 to fits its method to your data
errors_forward <- learnErrors(filtered_forward, multithread=TRUE)
errors_reverse <- learnErrors(filtered_reverse, multithread=TRUE)
then we visualise the estimated error rates
plotErrors(errors_forward, nominalQ=TRUE) +
    theme_minimal()

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Dereplication
From the Dada2 documentation:

Dereplication combines all identical sequencing reads into into “unique sequences” with a corresponding “abundance”: the number of reads with that unique sequence. Dereplication substantially reduces computation time by eliminating redundant comparisons.

derep_forward <- derepFastq(filtered_forward, verbose=TRUE)
derep_reverse <- derepFastq(filtered_reverse, verbose=TRUE)
# name the derep-class objects by the sample names
names(derep_forward) <- sample_names
names(derep_reverse) <- sample_names

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Sample inference
We are now ready to apply the core sequence-variant inference algorithm to the dereplicated data.
dada_forward <- dada(derep_forward, err=errors_forward, multithread=TRUE)
dada_reverse <- dada(derep_reverse, err=errors_reverse, multithread=TRUE)

# inspect the dada-class object
dada_forward[[1]]
The DADA2 algorithm inferred 128 real sequence variants from the 1979 unique sequences in the first sample.

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Merge Paired-end Reads
Now that the reads are trimmed, dereplicated and error-corrected we can merge them together
merged_reads <- mergePairs(dada_forward, derep_forward, dada_reverse,
                           derep_reverse, verbose=TRUE)

# inspect the merger data.frame from the first sample
head(merged_reads[[1]])

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Construct Sequence Table
We can now construct a sequence table of our mouse samples, a higher-resolution version of the OTU table produced by traditional methods.
seq_table <- makeSequenceTable(merged_reads)
dim(seq_table)

# inspect distribution of sequence lengths
table(nchar(getSequences(seq_table)))

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Remove Chimeras
The dada method used earlier removes substitutions and indel errors but chimeras remain. We remove the chimera with
seq_table_nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seq_table, method='consensus',
                                       multithread=TRUE, verbose=TRUE)
dim(seq_table_nochim)

# which percentage of our reads did we keep?
sum(seq_table_nochim) / sum(seq_table)
As a final check of our progress, we’ll look at the number of reads that made it through each step in the pipeline
get_n <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))

track <- cbind(out, sapply(dada_forward, get_n), sapply(merged_reads, get_n),
               rowSums(seq_table), rowSums(seq_table_nochim))

colnames(track) <- c('input', 'filtered', 'denoised', 'merged', 'tabled',
                     'nonchim')
rownames(track) <- sample_names
head(track)
We kept the majority of our reads!

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
section: Check the Result with the Mock Community
text:
Check the Result with the Mock Community
One of the samples, Mock, is not a mouse sample. It is a mock community: a mix of about 20 known bacterial strains, prepared in the laboratory and sequenced together with the real samples. We know what it contains, so we can check what our analysis does.
The file HMP_MOCK.v35.fasta of the data folder contains the true sequences of these strains.
# the sequence variants found in the Mock sample
mock_asvs <- seq_table_nochim['Mock', ]
mock_asvs <- sort(mock_asvs[mock_asvs > 0], decreasing=TRUE)
length(mock_asvs)

# how many of them are exactly identical to a true sequence?
mock_ref <- getSequences(file.path(path, 'HMP_MOCK.v35.fasta'))
is_exact <- sapply(names(mock_asvs),
                   function(x) any(grepl(x, mock_ref, fixed=TRUE)))
sum(is_exact)

# how many reads are in sequence variants that match no true sequence?
sum(mock_asvs[!is_exact])






TipQuestion



How many sequence variants did DADA2 find in the mock community? How many are exact matches to a true sequence? What does this tell you about the errors that remain after the whole analysis?








TipQuestion



A mock community can show two kinds of problems: sequences that should not be there, and strains that are missing. Which of the two did we check here? How would you check the other one?

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Assign Taxonomy
Now we assign taxonomy to our sequences using the SILVA database, release 138.2. The first step compares each sequence with the reference and gives a name down to the genus. The second step adds a species name only when the sequence is exactly identical to a reference sequence.






Warning



This step needs about 5 GB of memory and takes a few minutes. RStudio runs on your own system, not in WSL. On a Windows laptop with 8 GB, first give the memory of WSL back to Windows: close the Ubuntu terminals and run wsl --shutdown in PowerShell. Close the other programs too.


taxa <- assignTaxonomy(seq_table_nochim,
                       'MiSeq_SOP/silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz',
                       multithread=TRUE)
taxa <- addSpecies(taxa, 'MiSeq_SOP/silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz')






Note



The names depend on the release of the database. SILVA 138.2 uses the current names of the phyla, the same as the Kraken 2 database of Day 1: Bacillota (before: Firmicutes), Bacteroidota (Bacteroidetes), Pseudomonadota (Proteobacteria), Actinomycetota (Actinobacteria). Older tutorials and papers, and the Galaxy version of this tutorial (SILVA 132), show the old names for the same organisms.


for inspecting the classification
taxa_print <- taxa  # removing sequence rownames for display only
rownames(taxa_print) <- NULL
head(taxa_print)

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Phylogenetic Tree
DADA2 is reference-free so we have to build the tree ourselves
We first align our sequences
# use the table without chimeras: a chimera is not a real sequence and has no place in the tree
sequences <- getSequences(seq_table_nochim)
names(sequences) <- sequences  # this propagates to the tip labels of the tree
alignment <- AlignSeqs(DNAStringSet(sequences), anchor=NA)
Then we build a neighbour-joining tree then fit a maximum likelihood tree using the neighbour-joining tree as a starting point. This is the longest step of the tutorial: about 5 to 10 minutes.
phang_align <- phyDat(as(alignment, 'matrix'), type='DNA')
dm <- dist.ml(phang_align)
treeNJ <- NJ(dm)  # note, tip order != sequence order
fit = pml(treeNJ, data=phang_align)

# negative edges length changed to 0!

fitGTR <- update(fit, k=4, inv=0.2)
fitGTR <- optim.pml(fitGTR, model='GTR', optInv=TRUE, optGamma=TRUE,
                    rearrangement='stochastic',
                    control=pml.control(trace=0))
detach('package:phangorn', unload=TRUE)

title: Day 2: amplicon sequencing with DADA2
text:
Phyloseq
First load the metadata
sample_data <- read.table(
    'https://hadrieng.github.io/tutorials/data/16S_metadata.txt',
    header=TRUE, row.names="sample_name")
We can now construct a phyloseq object from our output and newly created metadata
physeq <- phyloseq(otu_table(seq_table_nochim, taxa_are_rows=FALSE),
                   sample_data(sample_data),
                   tax_table(taxa),
                   phy_tree(fitGTR$tree))
# remove the mock sample: we have used it above, it is not part of the mouse experiment
physeq <- prune_samples(sample_names(physeq) != 'Mock', physeq)
physeq
Let’s look at the alpha diversity of our samples: the number of sequence variants observed in each sample (Observed) and the Shannon index, which also takes into account how evenly the reads are spread over the variants.
plot_richness(physeq, x='day', measures=c('Observed', 'Shannon'), color='when') +
    theme_minimal()






Note



Other richness measures, such as Chao1, ACE or Fisher’s alpha, estimate the number of unseen variants from the variants that were seen only once (singletons). DADA2 removes singletons, because it cannot tell them from errors. So these measures have no meaning on a DADA2 table: do not use them here. This is also why plot_richness prints a warning about singletons: with DADA2 data, the warning is expected.


No obvious differences. Let’s look at ordination methods (beta diversity)
We can perform an MDS with euclidean distance (mathematically equivalent to a PCA)
ord <- ordinate(physeq, 'MDS', 'euclidean')
plot_ordination(physeq, ord, type='samples', color='when',
                title='MDS (PCoA) with Euclidean distance, MiSeq SOP samples') +
    theme_minimal()
now with the Bray-Curtis distance, and another ordination method (NMDS). This plot is not a PCA: its axes have no unit, only the distances between the points matter.
ord <- ordinate(physeq, 'NMDS', 'bray')
plot_ordination(physeq, ord, type='samples', color='when',
                title='NMDS with Bray-Curtis distance, MiSeq SOP samples') +
    theme_minimal()
There we can see a clear difference between our samples.
Let us take a look a the distribution of the most abundant families
top20 <- names(sort(taxa_sums(physeq), decreasing=TRUE))[1:20]
physeq_top20 <- transform_sample_counts(physeq, function(OTU) OTU/sum(OTU))
physeq_top20 <- prune_taxa(top20, physeq_top20)
plot_bar(physeq_top20, x='day', fill='Family') +
    facet_wrap(~when, scales='free_x') +
    theme_minimal()
We can place the sequences of one phylum, here the Bacteroidota, in a tree
bacteroidota <- subset_taxa(physeq, Phylum %in% c('Bacteroidota'))
plot_tree(bacteroidota, ladderize='left', size='abundance',
          color='when', label.tips='Family')
